_schema.status: verified = read from a cited source; method = a modelling choice, documented here; example = a stand-in shown as such in the app

tyre_longitudinal.model: Magic Formula, pure longitudinal slip (Sharp, Evangelou & Limebeer 2004, eqs. 1–6)
tyre_longitudinal.tyre: 160/70 ZR17 sport radial, fitted to test data reproduced by Pacejka
tyre_longitudinal.note: Table I. Used for both wheels and scaled to the surface by μ ÷ 1.2017; it is not a fit to the Royal Enfield tyres, for which no data is published.

wheel_spin_inertia_kgm2.note: Table A.II (Ifwy, Irwy), measured on a Suzuki GSX-R1000; used as stand-ins because Royal Enfield publishes no inertias.

pitch_inertia_kgm2.note: Table A.II: Imny (main frame, including the rider's lower body) and Iubry (rider's upper body), GSX-R1000; used as stand-ins about each body's own centre of gravity.

brake_capacity.note: Full lever gives 1.3 × 1.2 × (the most load the wheel can carry with the rider alone) × wheel radius: enough to lock either wheel on dry asphalt. Fixed for the motorcycle, so a pillion or luggage does not change it. Royal Enfield publishes no brake torques.

abs.note: A generic slip-band controller around the tyre model's own peak slip, not a manufacturer's algorithm.

unsprung_mass_kg.note: Table A.I: front wheel 11.9 + front suspension parts 7.25; rear wheel 14.7 + swing arm 8.0 (GSX-R1000), used as stand-ins.

tyre_radial_stiffness_N_per_m.note: Table A.V (fkt, rkt), sport tyres, used as stand-ins.

rider_sag.note: About 30 % of the travel used with rider (and luggage) aboard; the example value when your own sag is not entered.

suspension_model.note: Linear springs without preload, rates set so that the rider-aboard sag is as entered; damping as a fraction of critical, the same in compression and rebound (no published damping data for these bikes); stiff end stops at full extension and full compression.

powertrain.note: Stand-ins: 90 % from crankshaft to rear tyre, and the same losses oppose the flow of power when the wheel drives the engine; 0.15 s without drive during a shift; rev limit 1000 rpm above peak power; torque at idle 65 % of the peak. The torque curve passes exactly through the published peak torque and peak power; its shape elsewhere is an assumption. No motoring-torque or inertia figures are published for these engines, so engine braking rests on assumptions shown as such: with the throttle shut the engine drags with a torque that rises linearly with engine speed from 10 % of its peak torque at idle to 30 % at the rev limit (for the Himalayan 450's 452 cc, 4 to 12 N m, a motoring mean effective pressure of about 1.1 to 3.3 bar); its rotating parts (crankshaft, flywheel, alternator rotor, primary gear) have 0.012 kg m² at crankshaft speed; and the rider pulls the clutch in at 1.2 times the idle speed.

road_load.note: Air at 15 °C at sea level; rolling-resistance coefficient a stand-in. The drag area CdA of each bike with its rider is back-solved from its reported top speed, where the power at the rear wheel equals drag plus rolling resistance.

lateral_model.note: Stand-ins measured on a Suzuki GSX-R1000 and its rider (Sharp et al. 2004, Tables A.I–A.III), because Royal Enfield publishes no part masses or inertias. Wheels: Mfw, Mrw, Ifwx, Irwx. Front frame: the steered upper part (9.99 kg, Iff_str) plus the lower fork (7.25 kg) as a point mass, combined about their joint centre of mass, which lies on the steering axis 0.30 m above the front axle; inertias along and across the fork. Main frame (Imn, which includes the rider's lower body) for the motorcycle, and the rider's upper body (Iubr) for each rider and pillion. Products of inertia are tensor elements (Hx = Ixx·ωx + Ixz·ωz, z down), as in Meijaard et al. 2007.

rider_steering.note: The rider steers by handlebar torque from the lean-angle error and the lean rate, the controller form of Sharp et al. 2004 (section 6), with the torque the steady turn needs fed forward in place of their integral term. The gains give the closed loop a double root at −3.89 ÷ (the roll-in time), so that a step in the wanted lean is 90 % complete in about that time. The rider's arms deliver the torque through a first-order lag of 0.1 s, the neuromuscular delay for steering torque that Åström et al. 2005 report from a study of motorcyclists.

tread_rubber.note: Means of the three tread compounds in Table 1 (densities 1094–1137 kg/m³, specific heats 1.87–2.24 kJ/kg K); conductivity 0.3 W/m K as assumed there. Used for the whole tyre.

layers_m.note: Stand-ins for a road or adventure tyre; the tyre's band area and sidewalls come from its size.

hysteresis_to_tread.note: Stand-in: half the rolling-loss heat is generated in the tread, half in the casing and sidewalls.

road_surface.note: Stand-in properties of an asphalt surface, which set its effusivity √(k·ρ·c) for the contact conduction; only the real contact conducts, taken as 10 % of the footprint (stand-in; Miyashita and Persson note that the area of real contact is in most cases much smaller than the nominal one).

air.note: Conductivity at 10 °C and Prandtl number at 0–7 °C from the Engineering ToolBox; kinematic viscosity from the ISA sea-level values (1.789e-5 Pa s, 1.225 kg/m³); 0.5 m/s of air movement assumed at a standstill (stand-in).

grip_window.note: Stand-in for a road or adventure tyre; no maker publishes grip against temperature. Full grip from a 30 °C tread surface to 60 °C (Bridgestone sets road-tyre warmers to 50–60 °C and warns against 80 °C, the slicks' range; Pirelli gives 80–90 °C for racing compounds; Persson's group puts racing grip peaks near 100 °C and passenger-car rubber at a glass transition some 30 °C colder). Below the window the grip falls smoothly to 80 % at 0 °C and keeps falling below (Michelin: cold rubber stiffens and grips less); above it, 0.5 % per degree. Editable in the app.

riding_styles.note: Mean share of the available grip in use at each tyre over a ride, for the slip heat; the slip it takes comes from the longitudinal tyre fit (Sharp et al. 2004), used here for braking, drive and cornering alike, which probably understates the heat of hard cornering.

tyre_cornering.model: Magic Formula for motorcycle tyres in sideslip, camber and combined slip (Sharp, Evangelou & Limebeer 2004, eqs. 7–31)

front.tyre: 120/70 ZR17 front sport radial (measurements reproduced from Cossalter et al.)
front.note: Table II (middle row), Table III (middle row), Fz0 and the crown radius R0 from §§4.2–4.3, pDx1 and pDx2 from §4.5 (the other longitudinal parameters are Table I's). Angles in radians. Used as a stand-in for every motorcycle's front tyre: no such data is published for the Royal Enfield tyres.

rear.tyre: 180/55 ZR17 rear sport radial (measurements reproduced from Cossalter et al.)
rear.note: Table II (bottom row), Table III (bottom row), Fz0 and R0 from §§4.2–4.3, pDx1 and pDx2 from §4.5. Used as a stand-in for every motorcycle's rear tyre.

reference_160_70.note: Table II and Table III (top rows), the tyre whose longitudinal fit (Table I) the braking simulation uses; kept for reference and tests.

combined_slip.note: §4.4.1 and §4.4.2: the loss of longitudinal force to sideslip and of side force to longitudinal slip, fitted for the 160/70 at 3 kN and zero camber and applied to the 120/70 and 180/55 (§4.6).

surface_scaling.note: On another surface both peaks are scaled so that the peak friction at the nominal load equals the surface's μ (the side force by μ ÷ pDy1, the driving and braking force by μ ÷ pDx1), leaving the slip and camber stiffnesses unchanged, as the braking simulation does. The camber twisting moment is scaled with the side force; that choice is ours.
